name: Vinpocetine

lead: Vinpocetine is a synthetic derivative of vincamine, an alkaloid from the lesser periwinkle. It was developed in Hungary and sold there as Cavinton, and has been used for decades in parts of Europe and Asia for cerebrovascular disorders. In the US it is sold as a "nootropic" supplement.
Wikipedia says the evidence does not fully support a benefit in either dementia or stroke. There are no studies of vinpocetine for appearance.

paras: Proposed actions include sodium channel blockade, reduced calcium influx, antioxidant activity, PDE1 inhibition and inhibition of IKK, which affects NF-kappaB inflammatory signalling.

Reported effects include flushing, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn and blood-pressure changes. The FDA warned in 2019 that it may cause miscarriage or harm fetal development. US regulators regard it as an unapproved new drug and a 2015 analysis found many supplement labels inaccurate.

lead: Vinpocetine (ethyl apovincaminate) is a synthetic derivative of the vinca alkaloid vincamine, extracted from lesser periwinkle (Vinca minor) or Voacanga africana seeds.[1] Grokipedia (AI-generated) describes it as developed by the Hungarian company Gedeon Richter and marketed in Hungary as Cavinton from 1978.[2]

It has been used for more than three decades in several Asian and European countries for cerebrovascular disorders, though Wikipedia states that the evidence does not fully support a benefit in dementia or stroke.[1] In the United States it is sold as a supplement despite the FDA regarding it as an unapproved new drug.[1]
Its discussion in appearance-adjacent communities is as a general nootropic.
infobox: Unapproved new drug; sold as supplement

paras: Prescribed for cerebrovascular disorders such as stroke and dementia in various countries.[1] Registered trials have also looked at epilepsy[3], Parkinsonian disease[4], diabetic nephropathy[5] and fetal alcohol spectrum disorders.[6]

Postulated mechanisms include sodium channel blockade, reduced calcium influx and antioxidant activity; PDE1 inhibition and IKK inhibition have been reported in laboratory studies.[1] A 2010 paper reported that vinpocetine inhibits NF-kappaB-dependent inflammation through an IKK-dependent but PDE-independent mechanism.[7] Its poor oral bioavailability has prompted formulation research with lipid nanoparticles.[8][9]

Wikipedia notes that as of 2003 three controlled trials had tested vinpocetine in older adults with memory problems, and that a 2021 phase II open-label study examined sensorineural hearing loss.[1] Registered studies include a trial of NF-kappaB-dependent inflammation in acute ischemic stroke patients[10], a 610-person Chinese assessment in cerebral infarction[11], and a study of a multi-ingredient nootropic in healthy young volunteers.[12] Registry entries describe design, not results.

Flushing, nausea, dizziness, dry mouth, headache, heartburn and transient blood pressure changes are reported.[1] In 2019 the FDA warned that vinpocetine may cause a miscarriage or harm fetal development.[1]

The FDA treats it as an unapproved new drug, and tentatively ruled it ineligible as a dietary supplement around 2016-2017, yet it remains widely sold.[1] A 2015 analysis of 23 supplement brands found only 6 with accurate dosage labelling and 6 with no vinpocetine.[1] A US FTC action concerning the Procera AVH brand found marketing claims false and misleading and ended in a settlement with a permanent injunction.[1]
